blocks.x: Today we're recording a young lady. Could you give us your name?
Morelle.
That's all?
Denise Morelle.
Denise Morelle, I see. And we're in the Seminar Room 2 of the Howard Tilton Library at Tulane University. And today is May the...
7th.
The 7th. 1965 it is, yes. I can't remember the things. What we're going to ask you about, we're going to ask you about this train that they have built in Paris.
Yes.

You are a friend of Pierre Merlin and Pierre Atlan. That's how I found out about you. They wrote to me that you were coming. And you told me about that train. You want to say it in French? You want to describe it completely, including the mud?
I said it in French.
All right.

Well, their first experience with the train started in 10 years. They had to build bamboo and to get out of the holes in the middle of the table. And as there is a long way to go, there are little chariots that allow them to run under the table. And on the table, on the table, they have installed a whole and the American locomotive, the old, of the last century. And they tried to reconstitue the New Orléans in the last century. The ceiling represents the sky, it is blue with some clouds. On the walls, there is a campagin, all over with the trees. And there is the Mississippi, of course. There was a problem with the Mississippi, because it had to be as warm as possible. They tried to have the water tinted, color, with a sort of colorant brun. But it didn't happen because the colorant was placed in the bottom and the water remained clean. They put a kind of plastic plastic brun which imite very well the water. They are very happy like that. I suggested to put the real water, but they thought that it would not be. And then there are all the rues of the New Orléans. There is the gare, the waterfront, the French street, with the small houses, with the balcony of the fer forgers. There are the dogs, I already said, the Canal Street, and the campagnes, they also have made parks. But they stopped there because at the moment they haven't finished. They work a lot, they spend all their hours. So every morning, we see them with a marteau, a turn-in, working on the side, but it's never finished, and it never works. I haven't seen the train work. I haven't seen the train work. The decor is almost finished, but it's not that. I think it will never work. I think it will never work.
It's finished. It's finished. The trains never run. It's not that.
Yeah. But I wondered, are you going to take them any souvenirs back which they could use and to add on, you know, like advertising from packages, or anything printed they could put on the trucks?
As you want.

Well, we'll look as we go around. We'll look for things. You know, labels, I'm talking about. You know what I mean, perhaps. Do they use those already? Yes. They have those already. Do you remember any of the companies that they've saved? Do the names mean anything to you?
I don't know the names.
Yes, but they're typical New Orleans things, if they say, that's it. Did you say that you think they will finish it someday or not?
I don't think so. That's too much work, I think. I hope so.
How many nights a week do they work on it?
Oh, almost three and four. And the weekend, Saturday and Sunday too, when they are not playing jazz.
Do you see them often?
Yes. Or once a month. And more when .
When you hear them play? Yes. And they, but they don't play during the summer.
No. They play just in winter and spring, and they stop in May to October.
I see. Well, I wanted to ask you, you said Rabbanette is back with him, huh?
Rabbanette, oui. Rabbanette.
What is his full name? Claude?
Claude Rabbanette. I see.
Six months, you said, he'd been with them?
Six months, maybe more, from September, I think.
Yeah, I see. Yeah.
Also, you told me about the effect of Bechet on New Orleans jazz in France. How he changed.

Well, in fact, the influence of Bechet was really preponderant, because before him, of course, there was the Claude Luther's orchestra. There were some concerts with Louis Armstrong, who came to France, and who had a crazy success. But it was the arrival of Bechet in France, and the fact that he was fixed, that everything decided, that really created a terrible jazz jazz in New Orleans. At this moment, there were a lot of young orchestras who were created, who played, of course, with Bechet, and especially André Reveliotti. And Bechet, at the beginning, he did a little commercial music, I think, with the recordings like The Oignons, The Rue d'Antibes, and all that. And then, it had a good side, but it had a good side, because these recordings were commercial which allowed some young people to get interested in this music. And then, after, he played things less commercial, and the people liked it. The work was finally done, at the moment.
Did you... I don't understand French, Edwin. Do you have many old Bechet records? Have you heard many of his old records?
Oh, yes.
Do you think he changed?
Yes.
Is that what you were saying?
No. It was more commercial in France.
Yeah, I see.
Go ahead with what you were saying. I interrupted you there. Well, I think it was a symbol of Bechet. Because he had a lot of importance. It was a symbol of Bechet.
Because he had a lot of importance. After his death, it was almost done. It was a symbol of Bechet. And then, after what you were saying, I interrupted you there.

Well, I think it was a symbol of Bechet. I said that it was actually allowed many young French people to be interested in the Jazz Nouvelle Orléans. And, unfortunately, when he died... In fact, it was a symbol of Bechet. Because he had a lot of importance. After his death, it was almost done. It was almost done. There were still some orchestras who played, some young people who interested, but many less. And I think that the death of Bechet and the death of Reveliotti, a little after him. Reveliotti, they played very long with Bechet, three years, I think. After that Bechet had ceased to play with Luther, he played with Reveliotti, always. And the death of Bechet and Reveliotti were the end of a certain form of jazz in France. In fact, Bechet, when he was in France, he didn't really play the old style Nouvelle Orléans as you can listen to here or like Jospin, Merlin and Atlan. It was already more modern. It was already the same theme. It was more modern in the style and in the choice of the theme, I think. It wasn't the orchestras, the parade, the things of that genre. With the blues, obviously, it was always the blues. But all the themes that I heard, recorded by Bechet, during the time he played in France, were more recent themes. And often the compositions that he had made just before his death, or when he was in France. And he played, finally, pretty few themes. Except, obviously, Scratch Trumble or White Society, when people asked him, because people knew his airs, so they asked him. But, otherwise, he didn't play the same airs, even when I heard him record in the 1930s or before, 1925, when he played with... What do they call him? When he recorded with Armstrong, Charles Williams, all that.

I, uh... You finished? I think so. There are some things I wasn't sure if you discussed there. And, uh... Did you explain the difference between the young audiences and the old audiences? And, uh, the amount of interest, how intensely they're interested?

No. Not exactly. Uh... In France, uh... I think that the... The people of a certain age, they don't care about jazz. It's only the young. But the people of 40, 50, 60, or 60, don't care about jazz. Not like here, because I saw, here at the Fashion Hall, a lot of people of 40 or 50 years. In France, not at all. It's only the young. Mm-hm. by the modes. So, it was 10 years ago, it was the mode of the Jazz New Orleans. Bechet was at the mode, we were listening to Bechet and we were listening to Bechet. Now Bechet is dead, the rock and roll and the twist are coming, and now we are listening to the rock and roll and the twist. And the few of the people who listen to the Jazz New Orleans at Paris are often from the Irish, the Germans, the Italians, the Anglers, many English, but rarely French. Or, it's the young people who are here a little by chance, maybe because they knew someone in the orchestra, because they were more sentimentally, because they had a different culture. But the young people in general, the mass, the majority of the young people, they were interested in the music, well, yeah, yeah, like we used to play in France, that's-to-dire the Johnny Hallyday, and other Beatles, Animals, Surf, and things like that.
Yeah. But, again, I keep changing the subject, excuse me. But when Bechet was alive, did you ever see a jazz brass band in Paris or in Europe? No. Not even for his wedding?
Oh, I see the wedding of Bechet in Antibes. It was a big part, but a very French one, I think.
Yeah. No jazz bands?

Uh, yes. Well, there was the Luther Orchestra who played, but I have the impression that it was, you know, more French than American. Well, I haven't seen the paradis, I can't compare. But, after what I've been able to read, I don't think that it was the same thing. It was a very, very French, and especially very Mediterranean, because it happened in Antibes.
Uh, we were mentioning Boris Vian. Is that his name?
Boris Vian. Boris Vian, oui.
What did he play?
Trompette. En fait, he l'appelait trompinette, because it was a very, very small trumpet.
Smaller than a corner?
Yes. Very small corner, and he l'appelait trompinette.
And what style did he play?
What?
Did he play it?

Oh, yes. In 1945, he played at Taboo. He was the first musician French to play at the Jazz in New Orleans. In fact, I think he was the first, before Luther. Because he played during the war, at that time I was too young to know him. But I know that he started in 1945, at Taboo, to play jazz with others, before Luther started, because Luther started commercially in 1947 and 1948.
Did he get his inspiration from anyone? That's what I'm getting at. Did you say that? Did he have an inspiration? Armstrong, Oliver, Tommy Ladnere? Did he play like anyone or was he original?
Bix by the Beck.
He was like Bix. I see. So he was not the same style as Luther then?
Ah, no style, yes. Je n'ai pas compris. Non, pas exactement.
Not exactly. But he was well known.
Not very well. C'était une figure très pittoresque de Saint-Germain-des-Prés. But he was not a very good trumpet player.
And did you tell the other things he did other than play trumpet?

He was an engineer. He had studied math. He played trumpet. He wrote songs. He wrote very beautiful songs. They are now very popular. They are now completely popular. They are recorded by many singers. He had been singing by dear and he has never paid money with his books. He also wrote a theater piece. Very beautiful. And now we find him, a few years after his death, and there is a great fashion of Boris Vian, at Paris. We play his books, we have edited all his books, and his songs. He recorded some songs, as a singer. He wasn't a very good singer, but it was still a good singer.
What happened to people like Maxim Sari? What is he doing now?

Oh, he is very commercial. He is a very proud. He plays well with the clarinet. And he does good arrangements, I believe, because he has done long studies in the music Conservatory of Paris. But he lives with his music, and it's really quite commercial. But it's not bad, when he comes to the music. Well, he is certainly in the orchestra, in the only, in the two commercial orchestras, in the Nouvelle Orléans, in Paris, there is him and Luther, and I think that now, he is better than Luther, as well. Because Luther is not what he was.
Do you know, I don't know how to pronounce it. Claude Boling?

Claude Boling, oh, yes. Claude Boling, he is a wonderful pianist. He is also very, very proud. He has done extraordinary things. I met him when he was 14 years old. He was a little boy. He played piano in the surprise party, in the cassette of his parents, because he was not right. He was already a piano player. And he did his first orchestra, which was already very good, and which was at this moment, in a very New Orleans style, which was practically the same, that the style of Maxime Sorrie, and of Claude Luther. It was in 1950, but he has terribly changed, because he also, like Sorrie, he also lives his music. And he also does arrangements. He does music of films. He does music of a film, the Brigitte Bardot, and he accompanies Brigitte Bardot when she sings. And now he has a kind of a chorus of singers with him, with the girls who call them the Parisians, and who sing in the style Charleston, something of that kind. And it's very, very commercial. And it's not good at all. It's a shame, because he was a very proud musician.
And, uh... Do you like Johnny Dodds? Oh, very much. Well, what do most people in France, both of the jazz fans, think of Johnny Dodds?

Oh, he is very few known. In fact, the French people know the big names, that's to say Armstrong, obviously, Bichet, because he is here in France. But they know King Oliver very few, and Johnny Dodds, I don't think, but there are only some fans, some specialists who they know. And we have a lot of trouble finding Johnny Dodds in France. We know General Morton. General Morton was more known than Johnny Dodds. Maybe because the piano is a more commercial instrument than the clarinet, or more easy.
Well, what do you think about the New Orleans musicians who have come there in person? Have you heard Bonnie Bigard, Albert Nicholas, any of those? Yes.

The first time I heard Armstrong with Barnaby Bigard, I was a bit upset because I found that he was making a commercial music. It had a bit of a fabric, a lack of spontaneity. And when I saw Joe Killington when he was in Paris, it was even worse. I thought it was terrible. It was all except jazz. And they were very surprised by the exigence of the French public They thought that the French were more exigent. They thought that the French were more exigent than the American. And when they told them, they were playing the vieux air and they made an effort. Albert Nicholas, I heard him too. It was very good. It was very traditional and very old style. I think they had to tell them that the French public was exigent and they loved things very pure, the jazz very pure. They made an effort and the last musicians who came to come didn't try to make commercial. And in 2013, they tried to play what they wanted to play spontaneously, like they wanted to do it.
Did you mention Mesereau?

No, I haven't heard of Mesereau. He didn't play in France. He didn't play in France. He didn't play in France. But I think he was quite loved at some point. He came to... There was a fashion mode also, especially at the time when he wrote his book. And for a year, Mesereau was very fashion in France. And then, we talked about it. I don't even know what it became.

Did you... I couldn't understand much of it. Do you think that his fame is due to his writing letters to critics and his book? Did you say? His book, yes. Yes. But what do people think of his actual playing? Do they like his playing of his instrument?

Yes. He... Lorsqu'il est venu, oui, le premier concert qu'il a donné, il a eu beaucoup de succès. Mais... Ça n'a pas duré longtemps. Parce que Bechet est arrivé tout de suite après et Bechet a remplacé Mesereau dans le cœur des gens. He l'avait...
It didn't last.
Yeah.
As long as the book was popular.
Yeah. Did you think of anything that I asked? I'm running out of questions that I don't understand. Yeah. Range.
Mm-hmm. She was mentioning the fact that Bechet was playing a completely different style from what he had... Excuse me.
Charlie.

That he was playing mainly different tunes from his background. She thought he had changed his style that way, so very much by playing all these French tunes and tunes of the day. But I don't think this is entirely true. he was just following the old tradition. The musicians always played the tunes of the day. Oh yes. And what are traditionals now were tunes of the day then. Oh yes.
C'est vrai.
But the change in the audience is one of the things that changes people. Oui.
Yes. Yes. Yes. Yes. Yes. Traditionals. That's right. That's right. That's right.
That's right. I've run out of questions. I've run out of questions unless you have more to tell.
I don't think so.
Did we ask you about that? Back to the trains. When they work on the trains, do they wear the uniforms of the people? Oh no.
Yes. No, they're not.
Only for Christmas cards.
Yes. They sent a very nice Christmas card
showing a train, you know, with Atlan and his family and Merlin on the other side.

But they love the Reconstitution because the night of the 1st of July, we had a wake up with them and we were about a dozen. And they had transformed the apartment into a loon. And it's extraordinary because there were all the pictures on the walls. Wanted. Reward. The buffet of the dining room was covered with paper in a marble. It was a bar. They had absolutely demolished the whole apartment and Merlin had all decorated in a salon.
Well, maybe we should turn it off. I'll get it.

segments.title: Recording opening and the Paris model train project
segments.summary: Interviewer sets date and place; Denise Morelle is introduced as a friend of Pierre Merlin and Pierre Atlan, who built a model train in Paris.

segments.title: Merlin and Atlan's unfinished train, souvenirs and work schedule
segments.summary: She describes the long build, doubts it will be finished, and how many nights they work on it; the interviewer asks about labels to take back. They play jazz only in winter and spring.

segments.title: Claude Rabbanette rejoins the Paris band
segments.summary: Clarifying Claude Rabbanette's full name and that he has been back with them about six months.

segments.title: Bechet's influence on New Orleans jazz in France
segments.summary: She says Bechet's arrival and settling in France sparked young orchestras, that his commercial records drew young listeners, and that his and Reveliotti's deaths ended a form of jazz in France. She notes his repertoire was more modern than Merlin and Atlan's.

segments.title: Young versus older audiences for jazz in France
segments.summary: Only the young listened in France, as a fashion; with Bechet gone, rock and roll and the twist took over, and New Orleans jazz fans are often foreigners.

segments.title: Bechet's wedding in Antibes
segments.summary: She describes Bechet's wedding as a big, very French and Mediterranean affair, with the Luter orchestra playing.

segments.title: Boris Vian, trumpeter and songwriter
segments.summary: Vian played a tiny trumpet, started playing jazz at the Tabou in 1945 before Luter, was Bix-like but not a good player, a Saint-Germain figure, and also an engineer, songwriter and playwright.

segments.title: Maxime Saury and Claude Bolling gone commercial
segments.summary: She says Saury and Luter lead the commercial New Orleans orchestras in Paris, and describes Claude Bolling as a gifted pianist now doing film music and Brigitte Bardot accompaniments.

segments.title: Johnny Dodds and Jelly Roll Morton known in France
segments.summary: The French know Armstrong and Bechet, but King Oliver and Johnny Dodds are little known and hard to find; Morton is better known.

segments.title: Visiting American New Orleans musicians in Paris
segments.summary: She found Armstrong with Bigard commercial and a touring musician worse, Albert Nicholas traditional and good, and says the demanding French public pushed visitors to play purer jazz.

segments.title: Mezzrow's French popularity and his book
segments.summary: Mezzrow never played in France but was fashionable for a year because of his book; his first concert succeeded, then Bechet displaced him.

segments.title: Interviewer's view on Bechet's repertoire and winding down
segments.summary: The second interviewer disputes that Bechet changed style by playing tunes of the day, saying musicians always did; they agree and run out of questions.

segments.title: Back to the trains: Christmas card and the apartment party
segments.summary: They don't wear uniforms while working on the trains; they sent a Christmas card, and she recalls a party where the apartment was turned into a saloon. The interviewer ends the recording.
